topic: Frontend stack + hosting for satishregonda.in (and raftwaters.in): framework choice, 2026 hosting pricing/limits, India edge performance, DNS/email, privacy analytics, forms, CI/ops runbook, total cost, and on-site search.
key_findings: Astro is at 7.3.1 on npm (published 2026-09-03); Astro 7.0 shipped 2026-06-22 with a Rust `.astro` compiler, Vite 8 / Rolldown, a Rust Markdown/MDX pipeline (Sätteri) and a queued renderer — 15-61% faster builds. Breaking change to be aware of: the Rust compiler no longer auto-corrects invalid HTML, enforces JSX-style tag/attribute strictness, and collapses newlines between inline elements.

Astro's Content Layer solves the exact Google-Sheets/Docs problem. A custom object loader gets a `LoaderContext` with `store`, `meta`, `logger`, `parseData` (Zod validation), `generateDigest` (change detection → incremental rebuilds), and `renderMarkdown()` (added in astro@5.9.0, turns a Markdown string from a Google Doc into HTML with no extra library). This is a ~60-line file, not a plugin hunt.

There is NO published Astro content-layer loader for Google Sheets or Google Docs on npm. I searched the npm registry for `astro-loader` and `@ascorbic` — the ecosystem has `@ascorbic/airtable-loader` 1.0.5, `@ascorbic/csv-loader` 2.0.3, `@ascorbic/feed-loader` 2.0.1, `astro-loader-pocketbase` 4.0.6, `astro-loader-storyblok` etc., but nothing for Sheets. We write our own; `@ascorbic/airtable-loader` is the closest reference implementation to copy the shape from.

Astro **live** content collections are the wrong tool here: they require an on-demand rendering adapter, use a separate `src/live.config.ts` + `defineLiveCollection()`, and explicitly do NOT support MDX or image optimization. Build-time collections + a rebuild webhook is the correct pattern for this site.

Cloudflare Workers static assets are the single most important pricing fact: "Requests to static assets are free and unlimited" on BOTH Free and Paid plans, and "There is no additional cost for storing Assets." The Workers Free 100,000 req/day cap applies to *Worker script* invocations, not to static asset requests. A pure static site on Cloudflare has no meaningful traffic ceiling.

Cloudflare has 22 named data-centre cities in India — Agra, Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Bhubaneswar, Chandigarh, Chennai, Coimbatore, **Hyderabad**, Jalandhar, Jamnagar, Kanpur, Kannur, Kochi, Kolkata, Ludhiana, Mumbai, Nagpur, New Delhi, Patna, Pune, Sambalpur, Udaipur — out of 348 cities globally, with a "Sub-50ms to 95% of users" claim. Hyderabad on-net matters directly: IITH colleagues, students and Indian collaborators are the primary audience.

Vercel Hobby is legally unusable for this project. Quoted verbatim: "Hobby teams are restricted to non-commercial personal use only. All commercial usage of the platform requires either a Pro or Enterprise plan." and commercial usage is "any Deployment that is used for the purpose of financial gain of **anyone** involved in **any part of the production** of the project, **including a paid employee or consultant writing the code**." If Divyansh is paid at all, Hobby is out. Donations also count as commercial. Hobby also cannot connect to a Git repo owned by a GitHub organisation.

Netlify's free tier collapsed in Sept 2025. New accounts get 300 credits/month with a hard limit and no auto-recharge. At the published rate of "1 GB web bandwidth = 20 credits", 300 credits ≈ **15 GB/month of bandwidth**. Legacy (pre-2025-09-04) accounts still get 100 GB bandwidth + 300 build minutes. Pro is $20/mo for 3,000 credits (≈150 GB).

Cloudflare Workers Builds: **3,000 build minutes/month free**, 6,000 on Paid then $0.005/min; 1 concurrent build free / 6 paid; 20-minute build timeout; 8 GB memory, 20 GB disk. Cloudflare Pages by contrast gives 500 builds/month free (not minutes). An Astro build of this site is ~30-60s, so 3,000 minutes is effectively unlimited.

Cloudflare now says explicitly on the Pages docs landing page: "Workers supports most Pages use cases and offers a broader feature set. It is Cloudflare's primary platform for building applications. **Start new projects with Workers.**" The Astro deploy guide agrees and confirms a fully static Astro site needs **no adapter** — just `astro build`, `dist/`, and a 5-line `wrangler.jsonc` with `"assets": {"directory": "./dist"}`.

The one Workers-vs-Pages gotcha that decides our DNS plan: "Workers does not support any domain whose nameservers are not managed by Cloudflare." Pages CAN take a CNAME from an external DNS provider. So choosing Workers means committing both satishregonda.in and raftwaters.in to Cloudflare nameservers. (That is a feature, not a cost — it unlocks free Universal SSL, free Email Routing and free apex CNAME flattening.)

Cloudflare Email Routing is free on Free and Paid plans: 200 verified destination addresses per account, 200 routing rules per domain, 25 MiB max message size, 30 domains per zone. This gives `satish@satishregonda.in` → his IITH inbox at zero cost. Outbound *sending* from the domain requires the Workers Paid plan — so replies will come from his IITH address, which is fine and arguably better.

Cloudflare Web Analytics is free on all plans and works on sites **not** proxied through Cloudflare (just a JS snippet before `</body>`), but the limit for non-proxied sites is 10 hostnames per account. Since we will be proxying through Cloudflare anyway, that cap doesn't bind us.

Vercel Web Analytics on Hobby is 50,000 events/month with a **1-month reporting window** — useless for a professor who wants to see year-over-year interest in a paper. Over the cap it pauses after a 3-day grace period and resumes only after 7 days. Pro is $0.03 per 1,000 events with a 12-month window.

GitHub Pages is disqualified by two hard rules: "If the account that owns the repository uses GitHub Free or GitHub Free for organizations, the repository must be public" (so the Google service-account plumbing and the whole content pipeline would be public), and prohibited uses include "commercial enterprises." Limits are 1 GB published site, 100 GB/month soft bandwidth, 10 builds/hour soft limit, 10-minute deploy timeout.

Pagefind is at 1.5.2 (2026-04-12) with `astro-pagefind` 2.0.1 (2026-07-03). Claim from pagefind.app: a 10,000-page site searches with "a total network payload under 300kB, including the Pagefind library itself," and "for most sites, this will be closer to 100kB" — because the index is chunked and only fetched on demand. Pagefind 1.5.0 replaced the old `pagefind-ui.js` Default UI with a Component UI.

Fuse.js is ~8.6 kB gzip (full build) / ~6.8 kB (basic), zero dependencies — but it needs the *entire* JSON index shipped to the browser up front. For ~150 publications plus a growing blog that is a 200-500 kB eager download on an Indian mobile connection, versus Pagefind's ~30 kB lazy first chunk.

Algolia DocSearch will almost certainly reject us: "We offer the free DocSearch program to public technical documentation and technical blogs" and applications are rejected when "content is non-technical in nature." A faculty homepage with publications is not developer documentation.

Next.js is at 16.3.4 and `output: 'export'` explicitly cannot do: rewrites, **redirects**, **headers**, middleware/proxy, ISR, cookies, draft mode, server actions, and image optimization with the default loader (you must write a custom loader pointing at Cloudinary or similar). Losing framework-level redirects matters because we need to redirect old Google Sites URLs.

Google Sheets API v4 quotas: 300 read requests/minute per project, 60/minute per user, no daily cap, 2 MB max payload, 180s request timeout. Currently free, but the docs now warn: "Exceeding the quota request limits is planned to incur charges to your Google Cloud billing account later in 2026." A build-time fetch makes ~5-10 calls per build, so we are ~3 orders of magnitude under.

GitHub Actions is free with unlimited minutes on **public** repositories with standard runners; GitHub Free gives only 2,000 minutes/month + 500 MB artifact storage on private repos. Linux 2-core x64 is $0.006/min beyond that. Since we need a private repo (Google credentials, draft content), budget from the 2,000 free private minutes — or push builds to Cloudflare Workers Builds' 3,000 free minutes and keep Actions for lint/link-check only.

Cloudflare Turnstile free tier: up to 20 widgets, 10 hostnames per widget, 7 days of analytics, and "Turnstile can be used independently without requiring other Cloudflare services." Web3Forms' docs state the access key is public by design — "REQUIRED: Your Access key here. Don't worry this can be public" — with hCaptcha free/zero-config but reCAPTCHA v3 and Turnstile gated behind Pro.

Cloudflare's Service-Specific Terms restrict free CDN use to serving "video or a disproportionate percentage of pictures, audio files, or other large files." An academic site with paper PDFs and figures is within terms, but we should not host lecture video or a large dataset mirror on it — those go to Zenodo/YouTube/IITH storage.
recommendations: **Framework: Astro 7 (pin 7.3.x).** Runner-up: Eleventy 3.1.6. Astro wins on four axes that matter for this exact site: (1) Content Layer custom loaders are the cleanest path from a Google Sheet to a typed, Zod-validated `publications` collection; (2) `<Image/>`/`<Picture/>` with sharp does build-time AVIF/WebP + auto `srcset`/`sizes` with zero config, which no other option gives for free; (3) zero JS by default — islands are opt-in, so the site can genuinely ship 0 bytes of JS on most pages; (4) it is the framework a future developer is most likely to already know. Eleventy is the runner-up because it is even lighter and has near-zero churn risk, but its remote-data and image stories are more hand-rolled and there is no type safety on the Sheets schema.

**Do NOT use Next.js.** `output: 'export'` forbids redirects and headers (we need Google Sites → new-URL redirects), forces a custom image loader (i.e. a paid third-party image CDN or nothing), and ships a React runtime on every page. It's the wrong shape and it makes the site more expensive and heavier for zero benefit. SvelteKit + adapter-static is technically fine but has a smaller hiring pool in India and no image pipeline; plain Vite means hand-building routing, RSS, sitemap and Markdown — a false economy.

**Hosting: Cloudflare Workers with static assets** (not Cloudflare Pages, not Vercel). Deploy `dist/` via `wrangler.jsonc` `assets.directory`. Rationale: static asset requests are free and unlimited on the free plan, Hyderabad/Mumbai/Chennai/Delhi PoPs are on-net for the actual audience, 3,000 free build minutes/month, and no commercial-use clause to trip over. Runner-up host: Cloudflare Pages (same network, allows external-DNS CNAME) if for any reason we can't move nameservers.

**Explicitly reject Vercel Hobby on legal grounds, in writing, in the handover doc.** If Divyansh is compensated in any way for building this, the Hobby plan's own definition of commercial usage catches it, and the remedy is a $20/user/month Pro plan forever. Don't build a professor's permanent web presence on a plan whose ToS we're violating on day one. If the client insists on Vercel later, it's Pro at $20/mo = $240/yr.

**DNS: move satishregonda.in and raftwaters.in to Cloudflare nameservers.** This is required for Workers custom domains ("Workers does not support any domain whose nameservers are not managed by Cloudflare"), and it's what makes the free Universal SSL (apex + first-level subdomains), free Email Routing, and CNAME-flattened apex work. Keep the domains registered wherever they are — moving nameservers is independent of moving the registration, and .in registrar transfers are slow and error-prone. Verify separately whether Cloudflare Registrar supports .in before proposing a registrar transfer; I could not confirm it.

**Apex + www: make `satishregonda.in` canonical and 301 `www` to it** with a Cloudflare Redirect Rule (free, runs at the edge, no Worker invocation). Same for raftwaters.in. Add both as separate Workers/Pages projects on one Cloudflare account — do not try to serve two domains from one Worker.

**Repos: two separate private GitHub repos, not a monorepo.** raftwaters.in is described as already 'ready' — it has its own history, its own lifecycle, possibly its own contributors (students), and it must be able to break without breaking the professor's homepage. A monorepo buys shared design tokens, which we can get more cheaply by copying a ~200-line `tokens.css` into both. If the two sites ever converge visually, promote the tokens to a tiny private npm package or a git submodule then, not now.

**Contact: no form. Publish an obfuscated mailto and one Cloudflare Email Routing alias.** Set up `contact@satishregonda.in` → his IITH inbox (free, 200 rules/domain). Render the address as text assembled in a tiny inline script or with CSS `direction: rtl` reversal so naive scrapers miss it. A faculty member's email is already public on the IITH directory; a form adds a spam vector, a third-party dependency, a deliverability problem and one more thing that can silently break. If he insists on a form later, Web3Forms free tier + Cloudflare Turnstile (20 widgets free) is the cheapest working combination — but the free tier gives hCaptcha only; Turnstile is a Pro feature there.

**Analytics: Cloudflare Web Analytics.** Free forever, no cookies, no consent banner needed, already inside the account we're using for DNS and hosting, and the one dashboard the professor might actually log into. Second choice if he wants nicer reports: Plausible Cloud Starter at $9/mo ($108/yr with 2 months free) — but that turns a ₹0/yr site into a recurring bill he has to remember to pay, which is exactly the failure mode we're designing against. Do not self-host Umami or Plausible CE: Plausible CE needs Docker + ClickHouse + Postgres and ≥2 GB RAM, which means a VPS, which means a server the professor is responsible for.

**Search: Pagefind 1.5.2 via `astro-pagefind` 2.0.1, run as a postbuild step.** It indexes the *rendered HTML*, so publications, blog posts, student bios and the RAFT page all become searchable with no extra data plumbing, and the network cost is ~100 kB for a site of this size versus Fuse.js shipping the whole index eagerly. Scope the index with `data-pagefind-body` on the main content region and add `data-pagefind-filter="year"` / `data-pagefind-filter="type"` on publication entries so he gets faceted publication filtering for free. Skip Algolia entirely — DocSearch won't accept a non-technical academic site, and paid Algolia is absurd at this scale.

**CI: build on Cloudflare Workers Builds (Git integration), not GitHub Actions.** 3,000 free build minutes/month vs 2,000 for a private repo on Actions, preview URLs per branch out of the box, and one fewer secret store to manage. Keep a thin GitHub Actions workflow only for PR-time checks (`astro check`, `astro build`, a link checker) so a bad Google Sheet edit fails loudly in a PR instead of at deploy.

**Google service-account secrets: one read-only account, credentials in Cloudflare's encrypted build environment variables, JSON base64-encoded into a single var.** Share each Sheet/Doc with that service account's email as Viewer — never make the source documents public. Rotate the key annually and immediately on handover; document the rotation in a 5-line runbook. Never commit the JSON; add `*.json` under a `secrets/` path to `.gitignore` and add a `gitleaks` pre-commit hook.

**Add a rebuild button the professor can press.** Create a Cloudflare deploy hook URL and put it behind a single-purpose Google Apps Script menu item inside the content spreadsheet ("Publish changes to website"). Otherwise the whole Google-Drive-as-CMS story dies the first time he edits a Sheet and nothing happens for a week. Also schedule a nightly cron rebuild as a safety net — at ~1 minute per build that's ~30 of the 3,000 free minutes/month.

**Runbook for 'the site broke and Divyansh is unreachable': (1) roll back.** Cloudflare Workers supports rollbacks from the dashboard — Deployments → previous version → Rollback. That fixes 90% of incidents in 60 seconds without touching code. **(2) If a Google Sheet edit broke the build,** the build log names the failing row and column because `parseData` validates against the Zod schema; undo the edit in Sheets' version history and re-trigger. **(3) If DNS broke,** everything is in one Cloudflare zone; the previous record set is in the audit log. Write this as a one-page PDF, give a named IITH colleague or PhD student read/write access to the Cloudflare account and the GitHub repo, and store the recovery codes somewhere the professor controls. A site whose bus factor is one is not delivered.

**Total realistic annual cost: the two domain renewals and nothing else.** Hosting ₹0 (Cloudflare Workers static assets, free+unlimited), DNS ₹0, SSL ₹0, email forwarding ₹0, analytics ₹0, search ₹0, CI ₹0, forms ₹0. Budget roughly ₹800-1,500/yr per .in domain at renewal (UNVERIFIED — check the actual renewal price at his registrar; .in renewals are frequently 3-5× the first-year promo price). If he later wants Plausible, add $108/yr. The design goal should be: if every payment method on file expires, the site keeps serving.

**Set up spend protection anyway.** Even though the free path has no billing, put a Cloudflare notification on the account and make sure no credit card is attached to a plan that can auto-upgrade. The failure mode we are protecting against is a professor discovering an unexpected charge three years from now and letting the whole thing lapse.

## 1. Framework comparison — verified facts

### Astro (RECOMMENDED)
- **Current version: 7.3.1**, published 2026-09-03 (npm registry API). Astro **7.0 released 2026-06-22**.
- Astro 7.0 headline (from https://astro.build/blog/astro-7/): Rust `.astro` compiler replacing the Go one; Markdown/MDX via **Sätteri** (Rust pipeline); queued rendering engine ~2.4× faster than recursive; **Vite 8 with the Rolldown bundler**. Net: **"15-61% faster"** builds. New `src/fetch.ts` entrypoint for full request-pipeline control (Hono middleware compatible). Route caching now **stable** — "a single platform-agnostic API for caching" with Netlify/Vercel/Cloudflare providers. `astro dev --background` + automatic agent detection + JSON structured logging.
- **Astro 7 breaking changes** (relevant to us): the Rust compiler does **no automatic HTML correction** (invalid markup is now an error), enforces **JSX-style strictness** on unclosed tags/attributes, and **collapses newlines between inline elements**. Anything ported from a looser template will need a pass.

### Content Collections / Content Layer (the Google-Drive story)
- Content collections since **astro@2.0.0**. Built-in loaders: `glob()` (Markdown/MDX/JSON/YAML/TOML from a directory), `file()` (many entries from one file), plus **custom loaders via the Content Loader API**.
- `LoaderContext` gives: `store` (kv with `get/set/clear/entries/keys/values/delete/has`), `meta` (persisted across builds — sync tokens, timestamps), `logger`, `parseData()` (validates against the collection Zod schema *before* storing), `generateDigest()` (content digest for change tracking → **incremental updates across builds**), **`renderMarkdown()` — added in `astro@5.9.0`** (converts a Markdown string to HTML with metadata; this is what turns a Google Doc export into a rendered blog post with no extra dependency), `watcher` (dev-mode FS reload), `config`.
- Canonical remote-loader shape from the docs:
```ts
import type { Loader } from 'astro/loaders';
import { z } from 'astro/zod';

export function feedLoader(options: { url: string; apiKey: string }) {
  const feedUrl = new URL(options.url);
  return {
    name: "feed-loader",
    load: async ({ store, parseData, generateDigest, logger }) => {
      logger.info("Loading posts");
      const response = await fetch(feedUrl, {
        headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${options.apiKey}` }
      });
      const feed = await response.json();
      store.clear();
      for (const item of feed.items) {
        const id = item.guid;
        const data = await parseData({ id, data: item });
        const digest = generateDigest(data);
        store.set({ id, data, digest });
      }
    },
    schema: z.object({
      title: z.string(),
      description: z.string().optional(),
      pubDate: z.string(),
    })
  } satisfies Loader;
}
```
This is exactly the shape of the `googleSheetLoader()` we need. Swap the fetch for `sheets.spreadsheets.values.get`, use the row's stable ID column as `id`, and `parseData` gives the professor a build-time error naming the bad cell.

- **Live collections**: separate `src/live.config.ts` + `defineLiveCollection()`, require **an adapter configured for on-demand rendering**, use `getLiveEntry()` and `export const prerender = false`. Per the docs table: live collections have **no MDX support and no image optimization**. Version attribution is inconsistent between the two doc pages I fetched (content-loader-reference says live loaders are `astro@6.0.0`; content-collections says `astro@7.0.0`) — **UNVERIFIED which is right**, but irrelevant since we want build-time collections regardless.

### Astro images
- `<Image />` (single, sets width/height to prevent CLS) and `<Picture />` ("Generate a `<picture>` tag with multiple formats and/or sizes"). **Sharp is the default service**; `passthroughImageService()` for environments without sharp.
- Responsive: `layout` prop (`constrained` | `full-width`) makes Astro "automatically generate the required `srcset` and `sizes` values". Global default via `image.layout`. `image.responsiveStyles: true` adds the global CSS.
- Outputs avif/webp/png via `<Picture />`. **"For prerendered pages, this happens during the build"** — i.e. free, no runtime image service, no per-transformation billing.
- Remote images need `image.domains` or `image.remotePatterns`; unauthorized remotes are passed through unoptimized. **This matters:** if we pull headshots from Google Drive URLs, we must either download them at build time into `src/assets/` (preferred — then they're optimized) or whitelist the Google host.

### View transitions
- Native cross-document CSS view transitions work with **zero added JS**: "They don't alter the core functionality of a multi-page application, nor do they affect any existing scripts or add additional JavaScript to your page load." Chromium-only for now.
- `<ClientRouter />` turns the site into an SPA: navigation interception, `transition:persist` state, fade/slide animations, fallbacks for non-supporting browsers, lifecycle events — at the cost of a client runtime.
- **Recommendation: use the native CSS-only path.** A page-load animation is not worth a JS router on a site whose whole selling point is that it loads instantly in Hyderabad on a bad connection.

### MDX
- `@astrojs/mdx` v8.0.0, official. Adds JSX expressions, component imports, `export` statements, frontmatter-in-template access, custom HTML element mapping.
- **Using MDX adds no client JS by itself.** Framework components inside MDX require an explicit `client:` directive. Interactivity is strictly opt-in.

### Next.js (App Router) — REJECT
- Docs version **16.3.4**, last updated 2026-08-25.
- `output: 'export'` **unsupported features** (verbatim list): Dynamic Routes with `dynamicParams: true`; Dynamic Routes without `generateStaticParams()`; Route Handlers that rely on Request; Cookies; **Rewrites**; **Redirects**; **Headers**; Proxy; Incremental Static Regeneration; **Image Optimization with the default `loader`**; Draft Mode; Server Actions; Intercepting Routes.
- Image optimization requires writing a custom loader pointing at e.g. Cloudinary — a third-party dependency and a bill.
- Losing `redirects` is a concrete problem: we need to redirect old `sites.google.com/iith.ac.in/satishregonda/...` paths and any legacy deep links. (Solvable at the Cloudflare layer with a `_redirects` file — 2,000 static + 100 dynamic rules — but it's a mark against Next.)

### Eleventy (RUNNER-UP)
- Stable **3.1.6**; **v4.0.0-alpha.10** in pre-release.
- Template languages: HTML, Markdown, MDX, JavaScript, JSX, TypeScript, WebC, Nunjucks, Liquid, Handlebars, Mustache, EJS, HAML, Pug, Sass, plus custom.
- Ships no client JS by default. Image optimization via the `@11ty/eleventy-image` plugin.
- Why it loses: no type-safe schema layer for the Sheets data, image plugin is more manual, and remote data fetching is hand-rolled `_data/*.js` files. Genuinely lower churn risk though — this is the choice if we optimise purely for "still builds in 2032".

### Hugo
- **v0.165.0** (the docs site itself reports being built with it; page updated 2026-06-18). "A static site generator written in Go, optimized for speed and designed for flexibility" — "renders a complete site in seconds, often less."
- Real drawbacks for this project: Go template syntax is hostile to a future JS-shop developer, and the data pipeline (`resources.GetRemote`) is awkward for authenticated Google APIs.

### SvelteKit
- `adapter-static` with `export const prerender = true` in the root layout produces a fully static site.
- Documented trap: **"You must ensure SvelteKit's `ssr` option isn't set to `false`. Otherwise, prerendering will save an empty 'shell' page instead of the fully rendered content."**
- No built-in image pipeline comparable to Astro's; smaller pool of developers who'd inherit it in India.

### Plain Vite
- Means hand-writing routing, Markdown parsing, RSS, sitemap, pagination, and the image pipeline. Not a serious option for a content site with a blog.

---

## 2. Hosting — verified 2026 numbers

### Cloudflare (RECOMMENDED — Workers with static assets)

**Cloudflare's own guidance**, from the Pages docs landing page: *"Workers supports most Pages use cases and offers a broader feature set. It is Cloudflare's primary platform for building applications. **Start new projects with Workers.**"* No formal Pages deprecation notice; Pages remains on all plans.

**Workers Free plan limits:**
| Item | Free | Paid ($5/mo) |
|---|---|---|
| Requests | 100,000/day (resets midnight UTC) | No limit; 10M included, $0.30/additional million |
| CPU time | 10 ms/invocation | 5 min max (30s default); 30M CPU-ms included, $0.02/additional million |
| Subrequests | 50/request | 10,000/request (expandable to 10M) |
| Script size | 3 MB gzipped | 10 MB gzipped |
| Env vars | 64/Worker | 128/Worker |
| Workers/account | 100 | 500 |
| Duration | — | "No charge or limit for duration" |

**Static assets (the decisive fact):** *"Requests to static assets are free and unlimited"* on both plans. *"There is no additional cost for storing Assets."* The 100k/day free cap only bites requests that actually invoke the Worker script — and a pure static site invokes nothing. Caveat: with `run_worker_first`, matching requests always invoke the script and, on Free, return 429 rather than falling back to assets when limits are hit. We won't use `run_worker_first`.

**Static asset limits:** 20,000 files (Free) / 100,000 files (Paid, requires Wrangler ≥ 4.34.0); **25 MiB per individual file**; no documented total-size cap.

**Workers Builds:** Free **3,000 build minutes/month**; Paid 6,000/month then **+$0.005/minute**. Concurrency 1 (Free) / 6 (Paid). **20-minute** build timeout. Build container: 8 GB memory, 20 GB disk, 64 env vars (5 KB each max). Deploy hooks: 10/min per Worker.

**Cloudflare Pages limits (for comparison):**
| Item | Free | Pro | Business |
|---|---|---|---|
| Files per site | 20,000 | 100,000 | 100,000 |
| File size | 25 MiB | 25 MiB | 25 MiB |
| Builds/month | **500** | 5,000 | 20,000 |
| Concurrent builds | 1 | 5 | 20 |
| Build timeout | 20 min | 20 min | 20 min |
| Custom domains/project | 100 | 250 | 500 |
- `_headers`: max **100 rules**, individual headers capped at 2,000 characters.
- `_redirects`: max **2,000 static + 100 dynamic** (2,100 combined).
- Bandwidth/request limits: **not specified** in the Pages limits doc — i.e. no published cap.

**Workers vs Pages compatibility matrix** (from the Workers static-assets compatibility matrix page):
- Both: custom domains, preview URLs, redirects/headers files, rollbacks, build caching, monorepos.
- Workers-only: gradual deployments, Vite plugin, remote dev, dashboard quick-edit, cron triggers, native Durable Objects, queue consumers, rate limiting, email workers.
- **Pages-only advantages (2):** (a) **Early Hints** natively (Workers needs the zone setting + manual headers); (b) **custom domains outside Cloudflare zones** — Pages permits a CNAME from a non-Cloudflare DNS provider, whereas *"Workers does not support any domain whose nameservers are not managed by Cloudflare."*

**Astro → Cloudflare deploy** (from the official Astro deploy guide): *"Cloudflare recommends using Cloudflare Workers for new projects."* For a fully static site: build command `astro build`, output `./dist`, **no adapter needed** (the Cloudflare adapter is only for on-demand rendering).
```jsonc
{
  "name": "my-astro-app",
  "compatibility_date": "YYYY-MM-DD",
  "assets": { "directory": "./dist" }
}
```
Then `npm i -D wrangler@latest`, `astro build`, `npx wrangler deploy` — or connect the Git repo to Workers Builds for CI/CD.

**Custom domains on Pages** (if we go Pages instead): apex requires the domain to be a Cloudflare zone with nameservers pointed at Cloudflare — "Cloudflare will proceed by creating a CNAME record for you". `www` can be a plain CNAME to `<site>.pages.dev` from any DNS provider. Watch for CAA records blocking cert issuance.

**Universal SSL:** *"By default, Cloudflare issues — and renews — free, unshared, publicly trusted SSL certificates to all domains added to and activated on Cloudflare"* — all plans including Free. Covers the root domain **and first-level subdomains** (`www.example.com`). Deeper subdomains need Total TLS or Advanced Certificates. Certificates are issued after the domain is active on Cloudflare nameservers.

**Network / India:** 348 cities, 8 regions. **India cities: Agra, Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Bhubaneswar, Chandigarh, Chennai, Coimbatore, Hyderabad, Jalandhar, Jamnagar, Kanpur, Kannur, Kochi, Kolkata, Ludhiana, Mumbai, Nagpur, New Delhi, Patna, Pune, Sambalpur, Udaipur** (22 cities). Claim: *"Sub-50ms to 95% of users"* — "95% of the world's Internet-connected population is within 50 milliseconds of a Cloudflare data center."

**Terms check (academic use):** Service-Specific Terms restrict using the CDN without paid services to serve *"video or a disproportionate percentage of pictures, audio files, or other large files."* No percentage is defined. A text-and-PDF academic site is fine; a lecture-video archive is not.

### Vercel — REJECT for this project

**Hobby general limits:** 200 projects; 100 deployments/day; **100 builds/hour**; 45-min build timeout; 100 MB max source upload via CLI (1 GB Pro); 1 concurrent deployment; 50 domains/project; build machine 2 vCPU / 8 GB / 32 GB disk; runtime logs retained **1 hour**. **"Vercel does not support connecting a project on your Hobby team to Git repositories owned by Git organizations."**

**Hobby fair-use monthly guidelines:** Fast Data Transfer **up to 100 GB**; Fast Origin Transfer up to 10 GB; Active CPU up to 4 CPU-hrs; Provisioned Memory up to 360 GB-hrs; Function Invocations up to 1M; **Image transformations up to 5K/month**; image cache reads 300K/month; image cache writes 100K/month.

**Commercial usage (verbatim):**
> **Hobby teams** are restricted to non-commercial personal use only. All commercial usage of the platform requires either a Pro or Enterprise plan.
> Commercial usage is defined as any Deployment that is used for the purpose of financial gain of **anyone** involved in **any part of the production** of the project, including a paid employee or consultant writing the code.

Enumerated examples: payment processing; advertising the sale of a product or service; **"Receiving payment to create, update, or host the site"**; affiliate linking as primary purpose; ads/AdSense. A note adds that **asking for donations falls under commercial usage.**

**Pro:** $20/user/month (developer seats; viewer seats free). Included: first 1 TB Fast Data Transfer, first 10,000,000 Edge Requests, 1 hour Edge Request CPU Duration. On-demand rates: Function Invocations $0.60/1M; Active CPU from $0.128/hr; Provisioned Memory from $0.0106/GB-hr; Build CPU $0.0035/CPU-min; Image Transformations $0.05/1K; image cache reads $0.40/1M, writes $4.00/1M; Global Config reads $3.00/1M, writes $10/1K.

**Regions/India:** 126 PoPs globally, 20 compute-capable regions. **`bom1` = ap-south-1, Mumbai, India** is one of them. PoPs terminate TCP and route over a private network to the nearest region; TLS is terminated at the region. So Indian visitors do hit Mumbai — Vercel's India performance is genuinely good. The blocker is legal, not technical.

**Vercel Web Analytics:** Hobby **50,000 events/month included**, reporting window **1 month**, no custom events, cannot purchase more; on exceeding, 3-day grace then collection pauses and resumes after 7 days. Pro: no included events, **$0.03 per 1K events**, 12-month window, custom events with 2 properties. Web Analytics Plus add-on **$10/month/team** → 24-month window, 8 properties, UTM parameters.

### Netlify — REJECT (free tier is now tiny)

Credit-based plans became standard for all new accounts on **2025-09-04**.
| Plan | Credits/month | Price |
|---|---|---|
| Free | **300** | $0 |
| Pro (base) | 3,000 | $20/mo |
| Pro (higher tiers) | 5,000–20,000 | $33–$126/mo |

Conversion rates: **web bandwidth 1 GB = 20 credits**; database bandwidth 1 GB = 20 credits; **web requests 10,000 = 2 credits**; functions/preview-server/agent/database compute 1 GB-hour = 10 credits.

→ **300 credits ≈ 15 GB of bandwidth/month.** Free plan is a **hard limit with no auto-recharge**; you're cut off until the cycle resets. Personal auto-recharge is 500 credits/$5; Pro is 1,500 credits/$10.

Legacy plans (accounts created before 2025-09-04): Free = **100 GB bandwidth + 300 build minutes + 1 concurrent build**, hard limits; Starter had soft limits with overage at **$55 per 100 GB** and **$7 per 500 build minutes**.

### GitHub Pages — REJECT
- Source repo limit 1 GB (recommended); **published site ≤ 1 GB**; **bandwidth soft limit 100 GB/month**; **10 builds/hour** soft limit (does not apply when using custom GitHub Actions); **10-minute** deployment timeout.
- Prohibited uses include **"commercial enterprises, e-commerce, or SaaS"** and "sensitive transactions like sending passwords or credit card numbers."
- **"If the account that owns the repository uses GitHub Free or GitHub Free for organizations, the repository must be public."** Fatal: our repo carries Google service-account plumbing and unpublished draft content.
- One user/org Pages site per account; one project site per repository.
- HTTPS: *"All GitHub Pages sites, including sites that are correctly configured with a custom domain, support HTTPS and HTTPS enforcement."* Certificates via **Let's Encrypt**, auto-provisioned after a DNS check. "Enforce HTTPS" toggle in Settings → Pages.

GitHub recommends **always using a www subdomain**, "even if you also use an apex domain," since www isn't affected by GitHub's server IP changes. Extra A/AAAA/ALIAS/ANAME records on `@` **can prevent HTTPS certificates from generating**.

- *"Static sites are fast and free to deploy"* but they **count against your workspace's monthly included outbound bandwidth and pipeline minutes**, and **the docs do not publish those numbers** — you have to check the dashboard. Unacceptable for a handover doc.
- Custom domains included: Hobby 2, Pro 15, Scale 25; additional **$0.25/month each**.
- **Managed TLS certificates "always included for free"**, auto-issued/renewed via Let's Encrypt and Google Trust Services.

### GitHub Actions billing (relevant either way)

- GitHub Free on **private** repos: **2,000 minutes/month**, 500 MB artifact storage, 10 GB cache per repo.
- Linux runner rates beyond quota: 1-core x64 $0.002/min; 2-core x64 $0.006/min; 2-core arm64 $0.005/min. Extra artifact storage $0.25/GB/month.

## 3. DNS, domain, email

- **Cloudflare Registrar:** supports "over 390 top-level domains" including .com/.net/.org/.ai/.app/.dev. **At-cost:** "does not mark up domain prices at all… you only pay the price charged by registries and ICANN." **Free WHOIS redaction** by default. Does **not** support IDNs. **Whether `.in` is supported is UNVERIFIED** — I could not find a supported-TLD list at any of the URLs I tried (`/registrar/get-started/supported-tlds/`, `/registrar/account-options/supported-tlds/`, `/registrar/tld-policies/` all 404). Check the domain-search box in the dashboard before proposing a registrar transfer.
- `.IN` registry is NIXI (registry.in). The site describes .IN as "One of the fastest-growing Domain in the Asia Pacific" but the page carries no eligibility, local-presence, registrar-list or pricing detail — **all UNVERIFIED**. (Practically: .in has no local-presence requirement and is sold by GoDaddy, BigRock, Namecheap, Hostinger etc. — but I could not verify this in this session, so treat it as unconfirmed.)
- **Nameserver decision:** Workers custom domains *require* Cloudflare nameservers. Pages does not (for subdomains). Since we want Workers, plan on an NS change at the current registrar. This is a ~5-minute change plus up to 24h propagation, and it does **not** move the registration.
- **Apex + www:** put both hostnames in the Cloudflare zone. Cloudflare CNAME-flattens the apex automatically. Add a free **Redirect Rule**: `www.satishregonda.in/*` → `https://satishregonda.in/$1`, 301. Redirect Rules run at the edge and do not consume Worker invocations.
- **Email forwarding: Cloudflare Email Routing** — free on Free and Paid plans. Limits: **200 verified destination addresses per account** (shared across domains), **200 rules per domain**, **25 MiB** max inbound message, **30 domains per zone** (Email Routing + Email Sending combined). Sending to verified destination addresses is free on all plans. **Outbound "Email Sending" requires the Workers Paid plan** — so the domain can receive-and-forward for free but cannot send as `@satishregonda.in` without paying $5/mo.
- **Second site:** `raftwaters.in` becomes a second Cloudflare zone + a second Workers project. Zero incremental cost. Cross-link with a canonical, permanent URL from the RAFT page on the personal site.

- **Cloudflare Turnstile — Free plan:** "Up to 20 widgets", "10 hostnames per widget", 7 days of analytics. Enterprise: unlimited widgets, 200 hostnames/widget, 30 days. Crucially: *"Turnstile can be used independently without requiring other Cloudflare services"* and *"can be embedded into any website without sending traffic through Cloudflare and works without showing visitors a CAPTCHA."* Privacy: *"Turnstile does not access, store, or transmit user communications, form entries, or other page inputs."* **Siteverify request quota is not published** on the plans page — UNVERIFIED.
- **Web3Forms:** "a simple tool to set up Contact Forms for Static Websites… Receive form submissions directly in your email inbox without any server or back-end code." Tiers exist: **Free, Starter, Pro, Agency/Team** — **exact submission limits and prices UNVERIFIED** (web3forms.com/#pricing returns 403 to fetch). Docs confirm the access key is public by design: *"REQUIRED: Your Access key here. Don't worry this can be public."* Spam protection: server-side filtering on all plans; **hCaptcha free and zero-config**; **reCAPTCHA v3 and Cloudflare Turnstile are Pro-only**; honeypot is deprecated and not recommended. Pro features include CC, autoresponder, 5 MB attachments, webhooks, domain whitelist, Google Sheets integration (beta), Telegram/Slack/Discord notifications.

- **Recommendation: no form.** An obfuscated `mailto:` plus a Cloudflare Email Routing alias. Rationale: (a) his email is already public via the IITH directory, so a form protects nothing; (b) a form adds a third-party runtime dependency, a deliverability failure mode, and a spam surface; (c) it's one more thing that can silently stop working while nobody notices. If a form is mandated: Web3Forms free + hCaptcha, with the access key committed (it's designed to be public), and route submissions to a dedicated alias so they're filterable.

## 6. Ops

**Repo layout (per site, private):**
```
satishregonda-site/
  src/
    content.config.ts        # collections: publications, news, students, alumni, posts
    loaders/
      googleSheets.ts        # custom Content Layer loader (Zod-validated)
      googleDocs.ts          # Doc → Markdown → renderMarkdown()
    content/posts/           # local MDX fallback for blog
    components/ layouts/ pages/ styles/
  public/
  wrangler.jsonc
  .github/workflows/pr-checks.yml
  docs/RUNBOOK.md            # the "Divyansh is unreachable" page
  astro.config.mjs
```

**CI split:**
- **Cloudflare Workers Builds** (Git integration) owns production and preview deploys. 3,000 free build minutes/month; 1 concurrent build; 20-min timeout. Preview URLs per branch. Protect preview URLs with Cloudflare Access if drafts are sensitive.
- **GitHub Actions** owns PR gates only: `astro check`, `astro build`, `lychee`/`linkinator` link check, `gitleaks`. On a private repo that's within the 2,000 free minutes/month; each run is ~1-2 min.

**Secrets:**
- One Google Cloud service account, **read-only**, with only the Sheets and Drive scopes it needs. Share each source Sheet/Doc with the service account email as **Viewer** — never make source docs "anyone with the link".
- Store the JSON key base64-encoded in a single Cloudflare Workers Builds **encrypted environment variable** (e.g. `GOOGLE_SA_KEY_B64`). Mirror it in GitHub Actions secrets only if Actions also needs to build.
- **Rotation:** annually, and immediately on handover or if the repo ever goes public. Google key rotation is: create new key → update the two secret stores → trigger a build → verify → delete old key. Four steps; put them in RUNBOOK.md verbatim.
- Never commit the JSON. `.gitignore` a `secrets/` directory and add a `gitleaks` pre-commit hook.

**Content refresh:** a Cloudflare **deploy hook** URL (limit 10 triggers/min per Worker) wired to (a) a Google Apps Script custom menu item in the content spreadsheet labelled "Publish changes to website", and (b) a nightly cron as a safety net (~30 of 3,000 free minutes/month).

**RUNBOOK.md — "the site broke and Divyansh is unreachable":**
1. **Site shows old content / didn't update:** press "Publish changes to website" in the spreadsheet. If nothing happens in 5 minutes, open Cloudflare → Workers → the project → Deployments and read the failed build log.
2. **Build failed after a spreadsheet edit:** the log names the failing row/field, because `parseData()` validates against the Zod schema before storing. Open Sheets → File → Version history → restore the prior version → re-publish.
3. **Site is broken/blank after a deploy:** Cloudflare → Workers → Deployments → select previous version → **Rollback**. ~60 seconds, no code required. (Rollbacks are supported on both Workers and Pages.)
4. **Domain not resolving:** Cloudflare → DNS. Compare against the screenshot in RUNBOOK.md. The audit log has the prior record set.
5. **Certificate warning:** Cloudflare → SSL/TLS → Edge Certificates → confirm Universal SSL is Active. Check for a CAA record blocking issuance.
6. **Bus factor:** add a named IITH colleague or senior PhD student as a Cloudflare account member and a GitHub repo collaborator **before** launch. Store recovery codes in a place the professor controls (not only Divyansh's password manager).

## 8. Search — verdict

| Option | Payload | Fit |
|---|---|---|
| **Pagefind 1.5.2** (`astro-pagefind` 2.0.1) | 10,000-page site: **"a total network payload under 300kB, including the Pagefind library itself"**; "for most sites, this will be closer to 100kB" | **Winner.** Indexes rendered HTML, so publications + blog + students + RAFT page are all searchable with no extra data plumbing. Index is chunked and fetched on demand — the first keystroke pulls tens of kB, not the whole corpus. Runs entirely in the browser on static files; no server. Works with "any static site generators and website frameworks" as long as the built HTML contains the content. |
| **Fuse.js** | ~8.6 kB gzip (full) / ~6.8 kB (basic), zero dependencies | Loses on data, not library size: the whole JSON index must be in the browser before the first search. For ~150 publications + a growing blog that's a 200-500 kB eager fetch on an Indian mobile connection. Only right if the search scope is *just* the publication list and we're willing to cap it. |
| **Algolia DocSearch** | n/a | **Not eligible.** "We offer the free DocSearch program to public technical documentation and technical blogs"; applications are rejected when "content is non-technical in nature." A faculty homepage is not developer documentation. |

**Implementation detail worth doing:** mark the main content region with `data-pagefind-body` so nav/footer boilerplate doesn't pollute results, and tag publication entries with `data-pagefind-filter="year"` and `data-pagefind-filter="type"` (journal / conference / preprint). That yields faceted publication browsing for free, which is the single most-used feature on an academic site — and it costs one HTML attribute.

exemplars.name: Pagefind (CloudCannon)
exemplars.what_works: The project site is itself the demo: search works instantly with no backend, no API key and no account. Documents its own bandwidth budget honestly — under 300 kB total network payload for a 10,000-page site, typically closer to 100 kB.

pitfalls: **Deploying to Vercel Hobby.** Vercel's own definition of commercial usage catches "a paid employee or consultant writing the code" and explicitly includes donation solicitation. Building a professor's permanent web presence on a plan we're violating from day one means the remedy is a forced $240/yr Pro plan — or a suspended site — at the worst possible moment.

**Choosing Netlify on the strength of a remembered free tier.** The 100 GB / 300 build-minute free plan is legacy-only for accounts created before 2025-09-04. A new account gets 300 credits = ~15 GB of bandwidth per month, as a hard stop with no auto-recharge. One paper going mildly viral takes the site down until the 1st of the month.

**GitHub Pages with a private repo.** GitHub Free requires the repo to be public. Publishing a repo that contains Google service-account plumbing, deploy-hook URLs and unpublished draft content to satisfy a hosting constraint is a bad trade, and the 100 GB/month bandwidth and 1 GB site limits are soft and unappealable.

**Choosing Cloudflare Workers and then discovering the nameserver requirement late.** "Workers does not support any domain whose nameservers are not managed by Cloudflare." If IITH IT or the current registrar has any objection to an NS change on satishregonda.in, we need to know that in week one, not at launch. Cloudflare Pages is the fallback (it accepts an external CNAME for subdomains) — but Pages can't do an apex without Cloudflare NS either.

**Using Astro live content collections for the Google Sheets data.** They require an on-demand rendering adapter, and the docs are explicit that live collections support neither MDX nor image optimization. Reaching for them turns a free, fully-static site into a metered runtime and silently kills two features we depend on. Build-time collections plus a deploy hook is the correct pattern.

**Fetching remote images at build time without whitelisting.** Astro passes unauthorized remote images through *unoptimized* rather than failing loudly. Headshots pulled straight from Google Drive URLs will ship as multi-MB originals and nobody will notice until an Indian mobile visitor waits nine seconds. Download into `src/assets/` at build time, or configure `image.domains`/`image.remotePatterns`.

**Adding `<ClientRouter />` because view transitions look nice.** It converts a zero-JS multi-page site into an SPA with a client runtime, re-introduces script re-execution bugs, and undoes the site's main performance advantage. Native cross-document CSS view transitions add literally no JavaScript — use those.

**Fuse.js for site-wide search.** The library is small (~8.6 kB gz) but the index isn't: the entire JSON corpus must be downloaded before the first search. Pagefind's chunked index is the opposite trade and the right one for a publication list that only grows.

**Applying to Algolia DocSearch and waiting.** The eligibility criteria are explicit about "public technical documentation and technical blogs" and rejection of non-technical content. An academic homepage will be rejected; budgeting time for the application is wasted schedule.

**Building the Google-Drive editing story without a publish button.** If the professor edits a Sheet and the site doesn't change until a nightly cron fires — or until Divyansh pushes — he will conclude the CMS doesn't work and stop using it within two weeks. The Apps Script menu item that hits the Cloudflare deploy hook is not a nice-to-have; it is the feature.

**Letting a Zod schema failure produce an opaque build error.** `parseData()` validates before storing, which is the point — but the error must be surfaced somewhere the professor can see it (a build-failure email, or a status line on a private `/status` page), or a single malformed date cell silently freezes the site at yesterday's content.

**Hosting large media on the free Cloudflare CDN.** The Service-Specific Terms prohibit using it to serve "video or a disproportionate percentage of pictures, audio files, or other large files" without paid services, and no percentage is defined. Paper PDFs and figures are fine; a lecture-video archive or a dataset mirror is not — those belong on Zenodo, YouTube or IITH storage, linked out.

**A monorepo for two sites with different owners and lifecycles.** raftwaters.in is already built and may be maintained by students. Coupling its build to the professor's homepage means a student's broken commit can block a publication announcement. Two repos, two Workers projects, one Cloudflare account.

**A bus factor of one.** Everything above is free and durable, and none of it matters if the Cloudflare account, the GitHub repo and the Google service account are all reachable only through Divyansh. Named second owners and a one-page printed runbook are part of the deliverable, not an afterthought.

**Assuming Astro 7's stricter Rust compiler will accept ported markup.** It no longer auto-corrects invalid HTML, enforces JSX-style tag/attribute closing, and collapses newlines between inline elements. Anything lifted from the Google Sites export or a third-party template needs a cleanup pass before it will build.
